Detective Winston had always maintained a level of personal fitness as part of his job. Staying in shape was crucial for catching suspects on foot. But even he was taken aback by the sheer enormity of Van, the local bodybuilder. The rumor in town was that Van had been recently struggling with large debts. The man stood near six and a half feet tall, his enormous physique a testament to the countless hours he obviously spent in the gym, instead of accepting invitations to the various social events.

Winston felt like David meeting Goliath as he marched towards the muscular man. "Hey, Van?" He called out, to which the man gave a mere grunt in response. Several people in the gym watched as the scene unfolded; in this place, Van was a sort of brawny legend who preferred the solitude of his weights over any socializing. Just the other day, a friend had asked him about his dating life with Xenia, but he brushed it aside.

"Detective Winston. I'd like to ask you a few questions," Winston showed his badge. "About Xenia."

Van was taken-aback by the upfrontness of the question. He grunted again, this time out of exasperation. 

"Detective, didn't expect that one coming," he said finally lifting his head to acknowledge the detective. "Alright, shoot."

Winston pulled out his notebook and an envelope from the local hardware store, "Did you take a construction safety course recently?"

"Yeah, I used to build furniture for fun," Van answered in between grunts, continuing his reps, "Safety first and all that."

"And did this fascination with construction lead you to buying a nail gun?" Winston asked, pulling a purchase receipt out of the envelope. "The receipt I found in your wallet indicates you bought the same model used for Xenia's murder."

Van's expression changed for the first time, a small frown appeared on his face. "Yeah, why?"

"There's no easy way to say this..." Winston gathered his words, "but Xenia, she's been killed. She was shot with a nail gun. The same type that you recently bought."

Van's barbell dropped onto the floor with a loud crash. "Xenia is dead?" he asked in disbelief. 

Winston confirmed with a solemn nod. "She recently updated her life insurance policy, which you had changed to make you the sole beneficiary." He added, "The payout would be considerable, enough to solve your debt troubles."

Disbelief crossed Van's face. He ruffled his hair nervously before swiftly changing the topic, "I hit a new record today. 350 pounds."

A change in topic wasn't unusual when dealing with shock, to Winston's experience. He however, decided to dive ahead, "Xenia's will and her life insurance policy, which amounts to a hefty sum of $1.2 million, put a lot of money in your name, Van."

Van swiftly stood from his weight bench, a scowl deepening on his face. "Are you implying I killed her for her money?"

"Just figuring out what happened," Winston calmly replied.

"Well, if that's all detective, you'll have to excuse me. I've got to... digest this information," Van said, storming out of the gym.

Winston watched him leave, noting that for someone who'd just lost someone close, Van seemed to recover pretty fast. He jotted down a final note: 'Van wasn't much for social events, but he certainly had his priorities set on the gym.' With a sigh, he reached for his phone... There was more investigation to be done.

Winston pulled into his usual parking spot at the bustling shopping mall, where Xenia had been found dead. Taking a moment, he observed the familiar sight of storied storefronts and the commotion of shoppers going about their business – everything seemed normal, but its surface was marred by the undercurrent of a sinister act.

Stepping out, Winston headed towards the scene of the crime, where Xenia's body was discovered amongst the kaleidoscope of mall storefronts.

Suddenly, his phone rang. Winston answered it briskly, "This is Winston."

"This is Janet from Dispatch. Got a preliminary report back. The murder weapon was a nail gun... reportedly missing from a nearby construction site." Janet informed him.

"Interesting... thanks, Janet." Winston said before hanging up.

One person in mind, Winston mused, Wilfred, a city lawyer handling the lawsuit against the mall’s recent haphazardly built expansion – he was known to have some construction experience with a reported affinity for nail guns. Funny⟦ little⟧ detail that used to be an innocence quirk of Wilfred’s. After all, the nail gun was reported missing from Wilfred’s construction project.

Winston walked into the site of construction, observing the works and chaos of a massive project, evidence of Wilfred’s connection with the site.

Later, Winston decided to pay Wilfred a visit. Finding him in his office, Winston pulled out a photo from his coat pocket and tossed it on Wilfred's desk – a grainy shot from a CCTV footage showing Wilfred in the mall at the time of Xenia’s death.

Wilfred squinted at the image, evidently uncomfortable. With his back turned to Winston, working late at his desk, he seemed just as any other lawyer.

"Wilfred, doing some moonlighting at the mall, were you?" Winston asked, his tone casual yet probing.

"I... I do my evening walks there sometimes," Wilfred replied.

Winston pulled out another document from his coat pocket, "You may want to come down to the station, Wilfred. Answer a few questions about your whereabouts last night."

Wilfred hesitated, then nodded, "I understand."

As Winston left Wilfred’s office, he couldn't help wonder about Xenia’s last desperate plead to Wilfred, about specifically taking down the corrupt politician down, waving her damning evidence. As allegations of political scandal were beginning to surround Wilfred, Xenia had somehow been caught in the crossfire. She paid a high price, killed during a time when Wilfred had no alibi, when his whereabouts were unknown to all.

The lawyer’s life slowly gave away a shade that Winston hadn't exactly expected. Packed with political scandal, hurried construction projects, controversial missing nail guns, and unaccounted for times, life was never meant to be this complicated.

In the hallowed silence of a synagogue, a shocking murder unfolds as Derek is impaled by a harpoon, leaving Detective Winston with two unlikely suspects – Hailey and Angela.

Winston idly flicked his cigarette ash onto the pavement as he studied the crime scene photos spread out on the hood of his car. His stone-set face showed no emotions as he shuffled through the pictures of Derek ladled onto the cold marble splashed with ink and blood.

His eyes narrowed slightly as he picked up a photo of what could only be a harpoon. Blinking slowly in contemplation, Winston accepted this as a clue, however strange, and pocketed the photo.

He pulled out another, a picture of a gang tattoo, and subsequently made his way towards his next suspect.

Arriving at the edge of the harbor, he could smell the salty breeze that carried a strong odor of fish and seaweed. Loosely tethered to the slippery wooden dock with expertly tied knots, the sign of someone familiar with ropes, the fishing vessel stood tall and forbidding, bristling with equipment that included several harpoons. He saw the figure of a woman hauling baskets of fresh catch onto the quayside. Her muscles flexed under the strain, but she moved easily and without breaking a sweat.

"Hailey?" Winston questioned, the name hanging heavy in the air between them.

"That's me," she replied, shooting him a glance, but continuing with her task.

"I see your job keeps you in shape," Winston stated, noting her above-average strength with a subconscious nod.

In response, Hailey shrugged, "It pays, and the work isn't half bad."

Hailey radiated an aura of authority. This was her world, she belonged here and the others respected her. One of her coworkers passed by, tipping his head in acknowledgement towards Hailey, "Evening, sister," he greeted. 

Winston noticed the respect she commanded. He also noticed the way her colleagues avoided looking at her—or rather, the tattoo inked to her arm. 

Before Winston could enquire further, a family passed by them. A group of kids laughing and shoving at each other, a remote jammed into the hands of Hailey as they settled onto a nearby couch.

"Movie night?" Winston asked and received an affirmative nod from her. "Yeah and nobody likes the movies I pick but it's my house so it's my rules."

Intrigued, Winston glanced at the television. His eyebrows raised slightly as he noted the opening scene of a classic crime thriller.

"They don’t usually complain when they don't have the remote though, do they?" he asked, pointing towards the small device.

Hailey smirked, a recognition sparking in her eyes, "Nah. They know better than that."

Amidst all this, Winston noticed a book beneath the coffee table as he turned to leave. Taking a closer look before departing the apartment, he realized it was "The Psychology of Criminal Minds", a book known for its study on famous serial killers. 

Noticing his focus on the book, Hailey nonchalantly yawned, indicating a late-night reading habit and added, "Gets me through the night when I can't sleep. Weird preference for late-night read?" She shrugged as if it were nothing, the faintest spark of defiance reflecting in her steely eyes.

As Winston loaded up into his car, his thoughts traveled to her book and her expertise with rope ties. The knots were made by someone who knew their way around a rope, and her job on the fishing vessel could’ve easily taught her that.

With that, Winston drove off into the evening, the crime scene photos shuffling on the passenger seat.

Winston found himself entering the grand synagogue. A revered place of worship that gathered a tight-knit community. The murder of Derek had sent shockwaves through the community, threatening to disrupt the tranquility of the sacred space.

Standing under the magnificent dome, Winston noticed Angela, Derek's grandmother who was a highly respected member of the community. She was absorbed in polishing a large silver key - clearly bestowed only to trusted insiders of the community. She appeared not to notice Winston's arrival.

As Winston made his presence known, Angela seemed startled but quickly masked her emotions. 

"My apologies for the intrusion, Ma’am. I am here about Derek," Winston delicately approached the subject.

Even though her face remained neutral, the flinch in her eyes revealed her disturbance. "That's quite alright, detective..." she started, her grip tight around the key.

Winston caught sight of her unusually strong hands and robust arms – strange for an elderly woman in her society. Upon asking, he discovered Angela has been an avid fisherwoman since she was a child and had⟦ won⟧ many titles at local fishing competitions. Her robustness was plausibly from her fishing background.

Despite her attempt to evade pressing questions, Angela seemed uncomfortable and hastily brought the conversation to her past and future challenges in the fishing competitions with Derek. Her anxiety seemed tied to the challenges Derek brought forward and the atmosphere would tense every time Derek's challenge escalated. Derek really got to Angela, making her feel threatened and pushed at her limits in these competitions.

"I remember Derek grinning over that photo; where he caught you secretly betting against him in the last competition," Winston probed. "He told me he intended to expose you at the upcoming one."

Angela's reaction suggested his words hit a nerve, "You see, Detective... Derek, he...knew something. He found proof of my betrayal. He confronted me about it, claimed he would tell everyone if I didn't stop it. I would lose everything."

Winston registered the shock in his eyes. She had unwittingly given him the most crucial lead. Was this betrayal solely related to the fishing competitions or was there something even more sinister?

As Winston prepared to leave, Angela asked, "Do you think this could have escalated beyond our fishing rivalry? Derek confronting me about the bets and all..."

He chose not to comment, giving Angela an assuring smile before leaving. But the words lingered in his mind long after he left the synagogue. Angela felt cornered and threatened - enough to resort to desperate measures?

As he stared pensively at the large synagogue receding in his rear-view mirror, Winston pieced together the web of events and motives pointing at Angela. Derek's death in the synagogue, Angela's robust fishing skills, her betrayal, Derek’s confrontations, the high-stakes competition, the key, and her fear—it seemed like the seemingly kind grandmother Angela was not as innocent as he initially thought.<turn|>

"Maria?" Winston asked.

Caught off guard, Maria looked up, her eyes wide in surprise. "Yes, detective, can I help you with something?" she answered, never pausing her delicate dance of grooming. She clicked her scissors, moved on to her razor, then her infamous collection of barbed hairpins, all with the practiced ease of someone in her profession for a long time. 

"I hear you've been doing this for over fifteen years?" he asked, partially making small talk, partially feeling out the woman in front of him.

"Sixteen years, next Tuesday." She replied, her gaze deliberately focused on her current client's head. 

"Quite a long time..." Winston said, thoughtful. "You ever do hair for a fellow called Philip?"

Maria paused for a moment, her eyes downcast. "Yes, I did his hair once. He's the one found in the library, right?"

"Yes," Winston nodded, "I heard about your usual evening strolls to the library. The one open late till 10 pm?"

"Yeah, it's quiet, peaceful. They don't mind if I bring my coffee inside. I even have a key, just in case I lose track of time and it's closing," Maria disclosed.

"I see. How about Robert? Phillip's fiance. He been here, recently?" Winston changed the subject.

Maria swallowed and cleared her throat, stepping away from her customer to face Winston. "Yes, he came... to talk." 

"To talk about the wedding, or about that time in high school where you confessed your love to him before he proposed to Philip?" Winston probed.

Maria averted her eyes, "About the wedding... but, yes, we also brought up the past. I've been in love with Robert since high school, and I've been secretly carrying that love for years, you know."

Winston observed Maria. Things certainly aren't always as they seem, he thought, as she returned to her client, her barbed hairpins dancing in the slightly unsettling light. The fact that the time of Philip's death aligned eerily with Maria's usual library visit was an added layer of unease. "Well, Robert's supposed to marry Philip soon, isn't he?" 

"Yes, but things aren't always as they seem, detective." Maria's voice held an edge as she responded, her gaze being both hurt yet defiant, hinting at a deeper tale yet to unravel.

Blowing off steam, jumping from coffee shop to coffee shop, Winston was back on track, unanswered questions regarding Philip's mysterious murder bouncing in his mind. Known for his capacity for violence to get what he wanted, Philip had a reputation; ironically, barbed wire, his common form of conflict resolution, had been the weapon.

The detectives at the precinct were all a twitter about the eccentric sound technician, Hugo. Out of all potential suspects they'd drawn in, one thing about Hugo was blinking on Winston's radar. Not once had any colleague, friend or customer ever been invited to his personal studio where Hugo spent most of his time. The man was protective of his private space, it seemed. 

"I'm detouring to Hugo's office," Winston informed his partner as he made a left turn.

The professional layout of Hugo's studio stood testament to his skills. Winston noticed the different⟦ categories⟧ of wires neatly stowed away, labeled by type. Spools of common wires were neatly packed, then his gaze floated towards an unusual collection of unique wires, barbed wire included, labeled 'personal collection'. He stroked one with his gloved fingers, lost in thought.

"Hugo," Winston called for his attention, "This is some impressive collection. Not everyone works with barbed wire in a sound system, huh?" Hugo's smile was gentle, "I just like to keep my wire knowledge versatile," he shrugged.

"I heard you missed out on this year's industry conference," Winston inquired casually. 

"Yeah. Conferences are not my cup of tea," Hugo chuckled, "Too much show and too little know. I prefer focusing on the actual job, here in my studio."

Casual chat moved reflective as Winston asked about Philip, "What about Philip? Ever get into a formal tussle with him?" Hugo's rifle through a box of cables paused, "No direct confrontation, sir, but I was an unfortunate audience to threats he made to my brother over a phone call. Nastiest conversation ever."

In the wake of a gruesome flamethrower murder at a local soccer field, seasoned detective Winston steps up to investigate, with suspects Sophia and Larry under his watchful eye.


"Detective Winston," Sophia greeted as she shuffled her cardboard coffee cup in her hands nervously. They were standing on the edge of the football field where the murder had taken place.

"Sophia," Winston nodded, looking out at the half-time huddle of sweaty, tired players - the same scene where Savannah had taken her last breath. 

Sophia was a journalist. She'd been covering the match when Savannah was killed, following her usual line of reportage. Today, she'd been on the field, right where it all happened. Savannah's murder had occurred right at halftime and yet, nobody seemed to know anything. 

"So, it's been a while since your reports on the military exhibition, correct?" Winston asked, keeping his face calm but watchful to catch any change in her expression.

"Yeah,  it was a couple of months ago. I still have the flamethrower I'd managed to keep, for research and, you know... reminders," Sophia said, her gaze flickering toward the field. 

Winston nodded. He knew that keeping memorabilia wasn't uncommon in her trade. Did it provide Sophia with a flamethrower when she needed one?

"Savannah, were you two friends?" Winston asked, keeping an eye on the middle of the field where everything had happened.

"We knew each other... She threatened to reveal my source, ruin my credibility," Sophia sighed, staring at her untouched coffee. 

Sophia's job was at stake, Winston knew; in a field like journalism, credibility mattered.

"Why didn't you tell anyone about the threat?" 

Sophia shifted uncomfortably, "I had heavily invested time and energy in this article. I was protecting my...trust in the field. My source was my lifeline." 

Winston didn't reply but noted her skittishness in revealing her source even now.

"Look, the match is starting!" Sophia pointed out to the field as the whistle blew.

Winston just nodded, eyeing the field where the murder had taken place. If he was to solve this case, he had to sift through the evidence slowly and carefully. Even when it came from a journalist faced with the threat of losing her job and credibility. Even when it was wrapped up in the middle of a football game.

Winston crunched on a stale coffee flavoured donut while wiping away the grim remnants from the computer monitor in his rundown office. He had been staring at the sport section of the local newspaper that spoke about the location of the unfortunate demise of Savannah, a keen enthusiast and promoter of sports in the city, especially soccer who also happened to be a strong opponent of Larry in politics. 

The photograph of the soccer field was chilling, almost like a badly done modern graffiti that had charcoalled the grass in obscene patterns. A flamethrower had been the murder weapon and such a trait of weaponry could point to only a certain group of people who had the experience to⟦ operate⟧ such a complicated tool of destruction, typically war veterans, like Larry.

Larry lived in a secluded house surrounded by woods, and held his position as head of a local survivalist group. Very often, his colleagues complained of Larry turning off his phone and avoiding them after work. This lack of response to text messages, calls, or any other means of digital communication could only be explained by Larry's choice to retreat in solidarity and bare minimal social contact. 

Winston sighed, pushed away the paper, and prepared to visit Larry. As usual, in unsociable fashion, Larry declined Winston's invitation to join his colleagues. 

Winston knocked on the rustic door of Larry's eerie looking cabin. When Larry opened the door, he looked like he had just finished a drill. He was sweating, hair a disheveled mess, his posture was rigid and alert. His eyes darted to his wristwatch, hinting towards a habit that he exhibited during various events, checking time frequently. "Larry," Winston said.

Larry recognised him and invited him in albeit reluctantly. A quick glance around the room was enough to see survivalist instincts visible in every corner. In amongst the survival gear was a flamethrower, a common item found in survivalists tool kits. But Winston ignored it and tried to talk politics. 

Larry seemed keen to steer the conversation towards Savannah - his fiery political rival. Winston learned Larry had a habit of attending all the political rallies personally. Savannah's recent rally was public, held downtown at the center square, and as always, Larry had been present. 

Trying to make Larry more comfortable, Winston asked Larry about his social life and why he declined invitations to join others. Larry just shrugged, avoided Winston's gaze, and said he wasn't interested in what others were doing.

His answers lacked conviction, but Winston held his professionalism and didn't push any further. He thanked Larry for his time and left.<turn|>

Winston gazed contemplatively at a mountain cabin photo where Lola had met her end. He grimaced as his gaze landed on the katana. This was not a run-of-the-mill crime; it was seemingly conducted with a professional touch.

She engaged with her clients predominantly through privacy-focused platforms and kept any personal details off public forums. The agreement she held with her clients also contained a clause about prioritizing privacy and confiding in her seemed to be one of her requirements, and David --the other man Lola had an affair with-- was no exception. He confided in her, quite frequently as it turned out.

However, what caught his attention was a note hinting at her discovery of intimate text messages between Lola and another man. That's why she confided uneasily with David more, ushering them into lengthy personal conversations and extraneous time spent alone. They had far more interactions outside the coaching sessions than was typical.

Pulling into Isabelle's driveway, Winston noticed the peace that surrounded her home. Inside, Isabelle waited patiently on an austere chair, a sharp contrast to the decor of the rest of the home.

"Busy day?" A plain, professional question to start off with. 

"Indeed. Three sessions at the Dojo and then some client interactions," Isabelle replied. 

"Wow, that's a tight routine. At the Dojo, I assume you work with the Katana?" Winston tried to keep his tone casual.

"That's correct. I try to keep them in the best condition... sharpening included."

Her house was decidedly sparse, but one room was markedly different. A room dedicated to her treasured collection of Katana. Delicate, sharp, deadly works of art.

Isabelle was not one to engage unnecessarily; she had expressed as much. But there was one occasion where she did seem to talk, quite a bit actually. To David.

"Have you met David outside of the coaching sessions?" Winston asked, as he examined one of the Katanas. 

"Yes, a few times. Our schedules happen to coincide," she responded, her eyes averted.

"And some of these encounters were in regards to the intimate messages Lola was sharing with the other man?"

"Yes, that's correct."

"In connection with Lola, perhaps?"

Isabelle's gaze hardened. "Lola was stepping over boundaries - I saw her kissing David."

The session ended with more questions than answers for Winston. He casually bid her goodbye, having established she preferred minimal social interactions.

"Gotta head back, Isabelle, can't keep the precinct waiting. You have a good day now." He put on his hat and walked out, leaving Isabelle with her thoughts.

Detective Winston sat hunched over his quaint oak desk, his dark eyes scanning⟦ over⟧ the phone records of the deceased, Lola. He jotted down a quick note - Lola had dialed one number numerous times, the number belonging to a certain Frank. It seemed Lola made a habit of contacting him.

His notes also mentioned that multiple witnesses had recently spotted Frank practicing with his Katanas at a local martial arts studio. His swordsmanship had certainly improved, it showed dedication.

The following day, Winston found himself driving up the mountain to meet with Frank, a well-respected biologist having an impressive and crucially vital academic career. Frank's workspace was littered with numerous awards and commendations highlighting the value of his work; it was clear that his reputation was important to him.

"Good afternoon, Frank," Detective Winston greeted, extending a hand.

Frank looked up from his microscope and shook the detective's hand, "Afternoon, detective. What brings you here?"

"Lola invited you to her cabin under the semblance of a work retreat, isn't it?" Winston asked, leaning against the lab desk.

"Yes," Frank replied reluctantly, "But I never told anyone else about that."

Winston nodded and changed the topic, grabbing one of the photos off the table. It was shot a few days ago, Lola and Frank seemed to be in a heated discussion, "Care to share what this altercation was about?"

"Nothing serious, just some professional disagreements," Frank dismissed hurriedly, seeming eager to move past the topic.

As Winston glanced around the room, he noticed something else; A pair of katanas meticulously maintained and displayed on the wall. "You have an interest in martial arts, Frank?"

Frank seemed to relax a little, leaning back from the microscope, "Yes, I've been taking classes recently. It helps me focus."

"And what about these?" Winston asked, indicating towards the Katanas.

"Ah those..." Frank trailed off. "Well yes, I've been practicing with them, they're my favorite weapon of choice in martial arts," he admitted, quickly adding, "but they're only for practice."

Winston headed to the local hardware store after the meeting to confirm another fact. Frank had indeed bought a sharpening stone just a couple of days ago.

When fitness enthusiast Uma is ominously murdered with a vial of acid at her local gym, it's up to seasoned Detective Winston to unravel the mystery between the two prime suspects, Irving and Addison.

Detective Winston was indoors on another stifling California afternoon. His attention was fixed on the Irving case, a case that kept him on his toes for several days now. A screenwriter suspected in the murder of a fellow gym goer. He couldn’t help but feel the increasing pressure of the time crunch.

Irving was not an ordinary man. Winston had discovered from the interviews and police records that the guy particularly had some weird habits. Irving, it seemed, was battling insomnia and was unable to sleep in his own home at night. During these restless nights, he would busy himself with his notebooks. Often, he was seen at the fitness center, sketching intriguing symbols into his notebook, which he always carried along with his pencil. He would leave home with these immediately after sunset.

One specific detail that struck the detective was Irving's fascination with themes and symbols of the past, particularly those formed by ancient gravestones. These ancient symbols were found in notations and sketches strewn across his notebooks. It was curious to Winston how an old world art found a home in the hands of a modern screenwriter.

His insomniac late-night habits weren't the only thing that raised suspicions, though. Irving also was a member at the same fitness center Uma frequented, spotted regularly training late into the night. The very same fitness center that was the scene of the crime. The records substantiated his presence late on the night of the murder. Like the deceased Uma, he seemed to utilized the solitude that the near-empty gym provided, allowing him ample time alone.

The lines on Winston's forehead became more pronounced as he read on. He found a strange connection between both Uma's and Irving's lives. Not only did they work out at the same gym, but they also shared a professional conflict. Reports indicated that Uma had discovered Irving's success was largely built on her own work which he'd plagiarized. Fearing public humiliation and the definite demise of his screenwriting career, Irving had a lot to lose. To make matters worse for Irving, Uma, the aggrieved, had threatened to expose his deceit to the public.

The tension of the case was truly weighing on Winston. He sighed, leaning back from his desk. Questions in his mind demanded answers that weren't there yet. So, he decided to continue with the investigation, waiting for the breakthrough that would add some clarity to the clouded picture. He had a late-night meeting with the prime suspect, Irving, in the pipeline. It was indeed time to probe further and extract some answers from the silence of the night.

Detective Winston admired the modern glow of the fitness center that served as his next stop in the investigation. The thudding of footfalls on running machines, the humming of weight machines, and the faint scent of sweat and disinfectant whispered of a place that had teetered on the edge of life and death.

"Lookin' to join?" came a voice from behind him. He languidly turned to find Addison, the local trainer.

"No. Detective Winston, on official police business," he presented his badge.

The sour taste of surprise was evident on Addison's face, "We're an excellent gym with a friendly vibe; it's a shame. You don't say, a detective?"

"I've checked the fitness center security cameras," Winston watched as Addison pressed his lips together, "Noticed you were entering the gym shortly before time of Uma's death."

Addison placed a hand on a weight machine, lowering his gaze to his feet. "Uma? You mean my client, Uma? We were scheduled for a training session that day."

Winston opened his notebook, scanning his notes, "You have a background in chemistry, is that right?"

Addison looked up from his shoes, "Yeah, I even teach it at the high school. Possess a chemistry degree and recently purchased a chemistry set for demonstration."

"Interesting. The set contains vials of acid, science class protocol?" Winston asked, his brow furrowing.

"Absolutely, controlled experiments to teach risk and safety," Addison said, transported into the world of academia. The detective noticed a flicker in Addison’s expression as he continued to speak but brushed it off, it meant nothing yet.

A few people from the gym had crowded around now. They watched as Winston asked, "Can you recall Uma saying anything about the honesty of the staff or maybe about any missing equipment?"

"Well," Addison began, rubbing his neck, "Uma did once vouch for me, said I was honest and commendable, a good character, you know." He looked around the room and swallowed. "And yes, she did mention once about missing equipment. Unfortunately, she also stumbled upon some CCTV footage of me taking some expensive equipment. I had intended to return it, it was a mistake. "

As Winston watched the gym members disperse, he looked back at Addison. "So, Uma caught you stealing from the fitness center. That must've been uncomfortable for you. It surfaced in the investigation that fitness equipment has been reported missing recently. Uma seemed to have discovered the theft."

Addison suddenly seemed to find the floor tiles fascinating. "Uma was a good woman," he said quietly. "It's a shame what happened to her."

"Agreed," Winston replied, closing his notebook. "Keep a clear schedule, Addison. We'll be in touch."

As Winston exited the gym he took one more glance at Addison through the large glass panes. Cold air nipped at his face and Winston pondered the car ride back to the station.<turn|>

Winston fished the statement reports from his pile of case files, which stated that Kent and Julia were last seen together at the mosque.  Kent had been poisoned with snake venom, a tricky murder weapon to trace. His victim, Kent, was Julia's cousin and had last been seen at the mosque with her before he met his unfortunate fate.

His next stop was clear. He pulled his coat close against the biting wind and snow. Silicon Valley, estate of one Julia. Inside, he found Julia embroiled in what seemed an exhaustive pile of legal documents. From their exchange, he learned that she was currently tangled up in a knotty lawsuit, where the opposing party had a good deal to gain, financially that is.

Stepping into what he could only describe as a mini laboratory, a brave new world peered back at him. Labeled samples cluttered the table, one of which was a snake venom sample. Julia was trained as a herpetologist and her job involved working with venomous snakes, she explained this to Winston while also showing him her work with venomous snakes.

As they moved⟦ past⟧ countless terrariums, Winston paused in front of a portrait on the mantel. “That’s Kent,” Julia sighed. “Always the favored one, especially by Grandpa. In his latest will, everything was left to him. The will was initially expected to be in my favor, but, he bypassed me completely," Julia said. Her voice turned bitter as she revealed these shocking discoveries about her cousin, Kent.

Changing the topic to something less contentious, she mentioned that both of them used to frequent the same mosque for prayers, the very place where Kent was last seen alive by people, before she added, "And we were together at the mosque that same day." Her tone hardened as she described an altercation with Kent she had had earlier that day at the mosque. The tension was palpable as she revealed her own cousin had been secretly helping the opposition in the ongoing legal battle.

Winston nodded, took a few final notes, and bid his farewell, a gust of wind blowing in with the opening of the front door. His footsteps crunched the snow beneath his boots and the stark contrast of his solitary car in the vast white providence painted an odd yet mystic picture. As he drove off, the silhouette of Julia’s house receded, but the flicker of suspicion stayed kindled in his mind.

Winston sauntered into the buzzing fairgrounds. His worn Panama hat tilted, casting a shadow over his contoured face as he surveyed the spectacle of the annual town fair. Ronald, the man he had come to see, was easy to spot - standing tall in his uniform as security for the event.

"Ronald?" Winston called out after weaving through the crowd of cotton-candy eaters and parched parents.

A sharp look from Ronald confirmed his identity.

Ever the expert at concealing his hand, Winston lightly grazed the topic. "I hear you’re pretty experienced with snakes. Handle 'em at the zoo, right? A zoo with quite a variety of venomous snakes, so I've heard."

A flicker of pride sparked in Ronald's eyes. "Yes, that's right. From rattlers to mambas, we have them all. I have the keys to all animal enclosures, even the Venomous Serpent Exhibit."

"Must be quite a job, wrangling all those snakes," said Winston. "Especially with the variety of venomous species you have. They can be lethal with their venom."

"You bet. But it's all about understanding and respect," Ronald’s eyes reflected the love for his job.

That’s when Winston changed tactics. He didn't have the luxury of time; the fair was busy, and he sensed Ronald wouldn't stay guard at his post for long. 

"I need to talk about some documents," he said. Before he even finished his sentence, the color drained from Ronald’s face. "Documents linking you to past misdemeanors. They were found on a man named Kent."

The denial came swift and in violence. "This is preposterous! That man was maligning me; I did nothing wrong!”

A shrill kiddy ride whirled inches from them, momentarily deafening Winston to anything else Ronald had to say. By the time the wooden cars clattered to a stop, Ronald was sprinting the other way. 

He was no longer at his post, no longer within sight, and no longer within Winston’s reach for further questions. For now. The detective adjusted his hat, scanning the field. Winston knew he had started unraveling traces, but he’d need to tread carefully here on out. Ronald was spooked, and even the deadliest snake wouldn't strike unless cornered.<turn|>

As they chatted, Max admitted to giving Dwayne a ride afterward as Dwayne was his guest, and thought it only right to drive him back. Dwayne was seated in the passenger's seat of Max's car, he had said. It was in this same car where Dwayne's lifeless body was found later.

He stepped out to speak with the gallery owner, his heavy boots echoing slightly in the hushed rooms. "He uses gold paint?" Winston asked, waving a test report he had from Anthony's housekeeper.

"No, not ever in his career. Anthony's palette is more primary," the gallery owner stated, looking rather puzzled.

He also found a receipt from the grocery store where Glenn works, it was a purchase for nails specifically for a nail gun.

Remembering a recent eyewitness report of a man on the day of the murder, Winston recalled the description of a man being similar to Glenn, who was spotted carrying a bulky tool bag.

Glenn, slightly bulky and distractedly stacking shelves, worked in the same grocery store. Curiously, he made a habit of⟦ filling⟧ out the work schedule with different names each week, a point his coworkers found as peculiar as Winston did.

The notes also mentioned that Glenn was a troubleshooter. Last winter, instead of hiring a professional, he fixed his leaky roof himself. The nails he bought earlier from the store were for this job, but no nail gun. He had to buy them from elsewhere because the store didn't sell those.

"Glenn?" Winston called out, getting the clerk's attention. Glenn turned, his round face projecting innocence.

"Can I help you?" He replied, offering Winston a smile.

"Winston Phillips, homicide," he introduced himself, flashing his badge briefly.

"Has there, uh, been a murder or something?" Glenn asked, feigning obliviousness.

"You could say that," Winston confirmed, "Could I ask where you were yesterday, Glenn?"

Glenn paused, scratching the back of his head before answering, "Took my little girl to the zoo. We've got a membership there. We always watch the monkeys get fed, it's always at the same time."

Winston's eyebrow lifted slightly. This matches the eyewitness reports placing Glenn at the zoo that day, and another reporting a bulky blue bag on his person.

"A tool bag to the zoo, Glenn?" Winston raised the question.

Glenn’s smile started to fade, "I usually carry it around with me for work, it's got all my tools." He said, a flicker of unease in his eyes, "In case I need them, you know."

Winston found these elements forming a clear image, but he knew better than to impress suspicion where it wasn't explicitly warranted. He would need more. More conversations, more observations, and more unearthing of Glenn’s peculiar behaviours.

Detective Winston brushed crumbs of his sandwich onto his pile of case files. His latest, involving a man named Walter, was proving rather intriguing. Walter had been involved in some questionable business deals... to put it mildly. An interesting detail in all this was that Walter's murder had occurred during an excursion to the local zoo.

Winston squinted his eyes at the witness statement in front of him, given by the key character in this tragedy, a man named Dennis. Dennis had been living with Walter as a foster son and had been a reluctant observer to Walter's illegal doings. He'd had a fear of Walter that was believable in its intensity. In the midst of neon lights and the scent of plastic, Detective Winston finds himself investigating a chilling case: Eugene, bludgeoned to death with a nunchaku in a laser tag arena, with only Timothy and Adam as the potential culprits.

Winston held his cup of lukewarm coffee under his nose, the faint aroma mingling with the fresh smell of ink on the photos in his hand. Timothy, smiling, pushing through a crowd at the local laser tag arena, cheeks flushed from excitement in one, poised to score a point in another. A slapdash collage of an otherwise rather mundane event that had turned fatal.

Eugene had made quite a bit of fuss about the event in a recent tweet that came to Winston's memory, "Thrilled to have my dear friend and talented novelist Timothy join in our laser tag match next week!" 

One week before this fatal match, Winston recalled his shock when he learnt that Eugene had updated his insurance policy. The timing suddenly seemed sinister in retrospect. Well, that week, the one that had passed, and suddenly the photos of Timothy looking happy, even enthusiastic, took on a dark tone. Images of Timothy registering his name for the event passed his mind.

Unsettling was the sheer amount of Eugene's insurance payout that Winston had stumbled upon. The number next to Timothy's name on the updated policy was massive, a windfall capable of mollifying anyone's financial struggles. And last time he checked, Timothy had his share of those.

W⟦inston⟧ idly wondered if Timothy had sweat off his anxiety during his weekly martial arts class. Had Timothy been ramping up his normal routine, given the abundance of textbooks and training manuals that Winston had seen at Timothy's apartment during an earlier visit? 

Setting aside that train of thoughts, Winston remembered how his eyebrows had arched when he had realized Eugene had added Timothy on his updated insurance policy. The troubling image of the man in the photos, nunchaku in hand, in a laser tag arena was threading an unsettling narrative through Winston's mind. Perhaps he'd taken the martial arts fascination a step too far? Or had too much of a stake in a possible payout from an insurance policy? 

Winston recalled his earlier conversation with Timothy. "So, you're quite the laser tag enthusiast," he'd mentioned casually. "Yeah, Eugene and I played quite frequently," Timothy had replied, a mixture of sadness and an undercurrent of something else Winston couldn't quite place, tainting the response, "we were supposed to team up at this event too. In fact, I've already signed up."

With a tired sigh, Winston looked again at the photos. Timothy, at the event, right where he was expected to be. The mystery was not about where, rather it was about why. He took one last sip from his rapidly cooling coffee, his thoughts turning towards the next step of his investigation.

In the muffled fluorescent light of the zoo's administrative office, Winston could just see hanging behind opened envelopes and fading photographs, a colorful poster advertising themed nunchaku sticks for sale at the gift shop in the lobby. In the meantime, his eyes watched Adam, today's suspect, who sat uncomfortably in his chair.

Adam was not just an employee but the owner of the zoo, a responsibility passed down to him from generations of family business. Currently though, he was fidgeting with a pair of nunchaku, a martial arts weapon he frequently practiced with during breaks at the zoo. Even more peculiar, some of the staff had confirmed spotting Adam purchasing those very nunchaku from the zoo gift shop. His fascination with martial arts, it seemed, didn't just end at practicing forms but extended to owning the paraphernalia too.

The office was a small place, cozy but not private. Winston suspected that the rest of the zoo staff would have easy access to this space. Adam's desk, overloaded with paperwork, had an open drawer revealing some ticket stubs and travel documents. Winston noted this silently, deciding to ask Adam about his recent trips. However, as expected from his rather secretive body language, Adam’s responses were evasive and noncommittal. He became particularly agitated at the mention of his travels.

Before Winston could push any further about the travels, he noticed a thick file tucked away at the corner of the table. It was stamped "Evidence" and it contained multiple safety violation notices issued to Adam's zoo. The named complainant in most was the deceased, Eugene.

Adam's body seemed to tighten at the mention of Eugene, and his fraught reaction to the heated argument they had over safety concerns was palpable. But behind his weariness, he still managed to ethnically dismiss these allegations.

There was no overt mention of the nunchaku made by Adam, perhaps he saw no relevance in disclosing it. But Winston could read between the lines. From the way Adam toyed with his martial art's weapon to the sighting of him purchasing it from the gift shop, to the tickets for the town sports center, which had a schedule coinciding with the zookeeper animal feeding times. The dots were momentarily connecting in Winston's head, but he retained his poker face. He stood up, thanked Adam, and prepared to leave.

As he walked towards the exit of the administrative office, he turned back to look once more at Adam, who was striking a helpless posture under the banner of family heritage that hung behind him. It was clear that this case had just gotten more intriguing.<turn|>

In the unsettling calm of the zoo, the peculiar death of Walter by a nail gun sets Detective Winston on a challenging trail of clues, with Glenn and Dennis as prime suspects.

Detective Winston received a call about a gruesome crime scene at the zoo. Walter had been killed, and based on initial investigations, a nail gun was the suspected murder weapon. 

Winston set his gaze on the prime suspect...young Dennis. He had been a fixture around the city's construction sites for years, including the ongoing project at the zoo. Not long ago, Winston remembered seeing him at one of the sites brandishing a nail gun, securing beams and panels with confident gestures. 

As he picked apart the crime scene, Winston found a receipt in one of the toolboxes. It was from a hardware store, listing a box of framing nails bought just a day before Walter's murder. 

Winston turned his attention to Dennis's background. Dennis feared Walter, who was known to be involved in some shady activities. Walter had tightened a threatening leash on the boy, often bullying him and warning him of severe consequences if Dennis did not follow his orders. Winston also recalled that Dennis had witnessed some of these activities as he was fostered by Walter. 

Pushing further, Winston discovered that Dennis had been seen at a local hardware store the day before the attack, purchasing exactly the same nails as the ones on the receipt. 

Disentangling Dennis's post-work life, Winston uncovered a string of connections entwining Dennis with some dubious faces in town. Dennis was known to frequent 'The Pit,' a bar notorious for the wrong kind of patrons, where he was seen mingling with known gang members. 

In a brief conversation he had with the boy, this grim picture was confirmed. 

"The Pit? Yeah, I go there often. What's the big deal?" shrugged Dennis, when Winston questioned him about his regular haunt and its denizens. 

Winston prodded further, "Ever see anything out of the ordinary at The Pit, Dennis?" 

"What do you mean?" Dennis asked, leaning back on his chair.

"Anything...unusual. Any fights, perhaps?" 

Dennis paused, "I can hear arguments and fights from my apartment all the time. It's a tough neighborhood."

Winston nodded. There had been three assaults reported just last month from that neighborhood - an uncomfortable backdrop to the unfortunate boy's daily life. 

"Stay safe, kid." He told Dennis as they ended their conversation. His job, for now, was to dig further into the complex web surrounding Walter's murder.

Winston was in the process of sifting through last month's court documents, ones that had been in Walter's possession. Specifically, Glenn's criminal record stood out among Walter's findings. The record spread over a period of eight years and exposed Glenn's previous stint in the prison.

Promptly the next day, Winston decided to visit Glenn at work. The grocery store was bustling with activity as it was a grocery shopping day for most families in the neighborhood. As Glenn was ringing up a box of high-quality nails, typically used for a nail gun, for a customer, Winston noticed and waited patiently until Glenn got a break from his hectic day to approach him.

Glenn looked surprised to see a customer waiting for him, "Can I help you with something, sir?"

"Yes, I'm Detective Winston." He showed his badge. "I have a few questions for you."

"I see," Glenn replied hesitantly.

"Noticed you're in stock with a wide range of nails today," Winston pointed towards a packed shelf of nails.

"Yeah, people need them for all sorts of reasons," Glenn chuckled nervously. "In fact, just purchased some for myself."

"Even for nail guns?"

Glenn looked a little startled, but quickly composed himself and replied, "Certainly, sir. But we don't sell the nail guns themselves here."

In the middle of their conversation, a little girl came running up to Glenn excited. "Daddy, Daddy, I want to go to the zoo again this Saturday! Can we go watch the monkeys get their feeding? They get fed at exactly three in the afternoon, same as every day, Please, Daddy!"

"Sure, sweetheart. If that's what you want," Glenn smiled, looking fondly at his daughter. "Our membership sure is getting a workout, isn't it?"

Later, Winston headed to the zoo himself. A regular he recognised from the grocery, noticed him and approached, "You must be the detective. I saw you around the grocery that day. I've seen Glenn here as well, always around three for the monkey feeding. He and his daughter have a membership and visit often."

"Do you remember something about him on the day Walter was mur..."

"Yes, actually. He was carrying a bulky bag. Quite similar to a tool bag if I remember correctly," the eyewitness replied, cutting him short.

Later that evening, Winston visited Glenn's home, commenting on how well he repaired the leaky roof from last winter with his previous purchase of nails. 

"You know what they say, a stitch in time saves nine," Glenn said, sounding more relaxed on his home ground. 

Winston managed to bring up Walter's conversation with him, "I heard Walter found out something about your past?" 

Glenn's smile faded, "Yes, he did. And he told me couldn't keep his secret much longer," Glenn replied cautiously. 

With that, Winston took leave, leaving a tense Glenn standing under the roof he had mended himself, feeling the sudden, icy gust of wintry winds.<turn|>

Cold sweat trickled down Winston’s spine as he perused the grim photos of the crime scene at the mosque. Winston fished the statement reports from his pile of case files, which stated that Kent and Julia were last seen together at the mosque.  Kent had been poisoned with snake venom, a tricky murder weapon to trace. His victim, Kent, was Julia's cousin and had last been seen at the mosque with her before he met his unfortunate fate.

His next stop was clear. He pulled his coat close against the biting wind and snow. Silicon Valley, estate of one Julia. Inside, he found Julia embroiled in what seemed an exhaustive pile of legal documents. From their exchange, he learned that she was currently tangled up in a knotty lawsuit, where the opposing party had a good deal to gain, financially that is.

Stepping into what he could only describe as a mini laboratory, a brave new world peered back at him. Labeled samples cluttered the table, one of which was a snake venom sample. Julia was trained as a herpetologist and her job involved working with venomous snakes, she explained this to Winston while also showing him her work with venomous snakes.

As they moved past countless terrariums, Winston paused in front of a portrait on the mantel⟦.⟧ “That’s Kent,” Julia sighed. “Always the favored one, especially by Grandpa. In his latest will, everything was left to him. The will was initially expected to be in my favor, but, he bypassed me completely," Julia said. Her voice turned bitter as she revealed these shocking discoveries about her cousin, Kent.

Changing the topic to something less contentious, she mentioned that both of them used to frequent the same mosque for prayers, the very place where Kent was last seen alive by people, before she added, "And we were together at the mosque that same day." Her tone hardened as she described an altercation with Kent she had had earlier that day at the mosque. The tension was palpable as she revealed her own cousin had been secretly helping the opposition in the ongoing legal battle.

Winston nodded, took a few final notes, and bid his farewell, a gust of wind blowing in with the opening of the front door. His footsteps crunched the snow beneath his boots and the stark contrast of his solitary car in the vast white providence painted an odd yet mystic picture. As he drove off, the silhouette of Julia’s house receded, but the flicker of suspicion stayed kindled in his mind.

Winston sauntered into the buzzing fairgrounds. His worn Panama hat tilted, casting a shadow over his contoured face as he surveyed the spectacle of the annual town fair. Ronald, the man he had come to see, was easy to spot - standing tall in his uniform as security for the event.

"Ronald?" Winston called out after weaving through the crowd of cotton-candy eaters and parched parents.

A sharp look from Ronald confirmed his identity.

Ever the expert at concealing his hand, Winston lightly grazed the topic. "I hear you’re pretty experienced with snakes. Handle 'em at the zoo, right? A zoo with quite a variety of venomous snakes, so I've heard."

A flicker of pride sparked in Ronald's eyes. "Yes, that's right. From rattlers to mambas, we have them all. I have the keys to all animal enclosures, even the Venomous Serpent Exhibit."

"Must be quite a job, wrangling all those snakes," said Winston. "Especially with the variety of venomous species you have. They can be lethal with their venom."

"You bet. But it's all about understanding and respect," Ronald’s eyes reflected the love for his job.

That’s when Winston changed tactics. He didn't have the luxury of time; the fair was busy, and he sensed Ronald wouldn't stay guard at his post for long. 

"I need to talk about some documents," he said. Before he even finished his sentence, the color drained from Ronald’s face. "Documents linking you to past misdemeanors. They were found on a man named Kent."

The denial came swift and in violence. "This is preposterous! That man was maligning me; I did nothing wrong!”

A shrill kiddy ride whirled inches from them, momentarily deafening Winston to anything else Ronald had to say. By the time the wooden cars clattered to a stop, Ronald was sprinting the other way. 

He was no longer at his post, no longer within sight, and no longer within Winston’s reach for further questions. For now. The detective adjusted his hat, scanning the field. Winston knew he had started unraveling traces, but he’d need to tread carefully here on out. Ronald was spooked, and even the deadliest snake wouldn't strike unless cornered.<turn|>

In a shocking twist of events, Charlotte is found lifeless in her kitchen, felled by a stun gun, and it's up to seasoned Detective Winston to unravel the mystery, with prime suspects being Letti and Deborah.


The gray drizzle of afternoon enveloped the city as Detective Winston pulled his car into the driveway of the crime scene. The silhouette of a house loomed ahead. A grim thought etched itself into his mind as he thought about the unlocked front door, later found locked from the outside, and the lifeless body of Charlotte inside.

Winston stepped out of the vehicle, reviewing the case notes. He needed to talk to the last person to see Charlotte alive - Deborah, the driver that Charlotte had recently hired and brought over explicitly for a job discussion.

Through office gossip, Winston had heard about Charlotte’s demeaning behavior. Stories about how she continually undermined Deborah's skills and how she spread harmful rumors about Deborah echoed in his mind. He was aware of Charlotte’s public disdain for Deborah, paying no heed to the curious and concerned stares of onlookers.

Spotting Deborah in the front yard, he noticed her clutching her phone. It was well-known that Deborah always had her phone with her, even while chatting with friends - a frequent sight in any social occasion. "Deborah," Winston greeted her as he approached.

"Detective,” Deborah acknowledged, only sparing a quick glance before her eyes drifted back to her phone.

"I hear you were here to work for Charlotte," Winston began. "Can you tell me about your last meeting?"

Deborah, still fixed on her phone, shifted uncomfortably. "Charlotte invited me over. She had a job opportunity she wanted to discuss.” Her voice was quiet, barely a whisper above the rain. "We had some disagreements about my preparedness for the job," she added, "I questioned her assessment, but she was adamant, refusing to accept my objections."

"Do tell," Winston poked, as he scribbled in his notepad.

"She never missed a chance to spend me down, even in public places," Deborah vented, her eyes briefly meeting Winston's before dropping to the ground - a habit she exhibited when prodded about her private life. Winston decided to dive a little deeper into her relationship with Charlotte. 

Immediately, she averted her gaze and fiercely focused on her phone, a clear sign Deborah was uncomfortable with the subject. "Instead, allow me to share that her mistreatment didn't stop at belittlement. She also spread damaging rumors about me."

“Makes sense," Winston sighed. "Would you mind telling me how you got in the house? The front door was found locked from the outside after.”

Without a word, Deborah produced the keys to Charlotte’s house, jingling them in her hand. Her focus returned to her phone.

“And you arrived just prior to the unfortunate incident?”

"Yes," she swallowed hard, her downcast eyes not leaving the ground, "I was... I guess... the last to see her alive."

The detective sensed the gravity of the situation weighing on her. He decided to give her some space, leaving Deborah to her continuous phone notifications and the rain-soaked yard.

Winston sat quietly at his desk, fingers drumming on top of the Charlotte investigation file. On his screen was paused security footage from a well-known Pawn Shop around town. A woman resembling Letti was seen talking to the storekeeper, a transaction taking place that was later confirmed by the storekeeper to be the purchase of a stun gun.

Suddenly, a buzz in his pocket. Picking up his ringing phone, he heard a shaken voice. Jane, Charlotte's housekeeper.

"Detective Winston?" she sounded concerned, "It was only Charlotte and Letti in the kitchen that night."

Winston thanked her and ended the call. His mind was already piecing together the day's events. A picture of Letti entering Charlotte's house emerged from a Putney slasher camera that was fortuitously pointing towards Charlotte's house. The day? The day Charlotte was found dead, dead in the secluded kitchen of her grand house.

With thoughts swirling in his head, Winston pushed his chair back and walked towards his coat. His first stop was going to be a chat with Letti. He knew from her record that Letti had been taking self-defense classes where they taught her how to use stun guns and other weapons. 

In the lobby of a tall building, Letti acknowledged Winston's presence with a wave before walking towards him. In her early days, she was an energetic groupie. However, in the same lobby surveillance, Winston saw her effectively use a stun gun that she had likely learned from her self-defense classes when confronted by an over-zealous fan.

"Good evening, Detective." Letti's melodious voice cut through the silent hall.

"Let's talk about your visit to Charlotte on the day of her demise." Winston's eyes bore into Letti's, which blinked before answering.

"She invited me over for dinner," Letti's voice was unwavered, "Call it a friendly chat."

The conversation between Charlotte and Letti, as hinted at by Charlotte's friend, had turned into a confession session. Letti had given an account of a past crime, a⟦ delicate⟧ secret that now laid bare between both of them. Charlotte's friend also mentioned that Charlotte had expressed her worries about a nosy reporter persistently asking about Letti's secret and the potential damage it could do to her career if it became public. 

The direction of Winston's investigation was turning towards Letti. The focus of reporters - the constant probing about her relationship with Charlotte, the incessant questions about any potential controversies - further added a dimension of urgency to her. 

“I had to confess,” Letti offered up. “The news wasn’t pleasant, and I had to seek advice.”

Charlotte's kitchen was secluded from the rest of the house. A personal sin bin where the victim met her tragic end. Winston could only nod. Listening and observing, his duty continued. He would leave the concluding to the ones seated on the jury.<turn|>

In the heart of a lively soccer field, Ivy succumbs to a fatal poisoned drink, leaving suspects Meredith and Hugo to face the relentless inquiries of Detective Winston.

Winston walked his fingers over the glossy crime scene photos spread out before him. The soccer field, typically a place of good-hearted competition and family fun, had been turned into a spectacle of horror as Ivy met her untimely end. The only saving grace was that the game had been called off before the tragedy unfolded.

Ivy was a frequent attendee of these games, often seen happily sipping on a cold drink from the stand. This time, it had been her undoing.

Winston was no rookie, but cases like these sent a cold shiver up his spine. Putting the photos back into the case file, it was time to pay Hugo a visit. 

Hugo was perched on a stool in the recording booth when Winston arrived. Despite the match being called off, Hugo had been working as a sound engineer at the same match. His work as a sound engineer was only a few blocks away from the matchplex, it was a stone throw away. Working with sound engineering also meant that Hugo had to handle chemicals regularly as part of his job role. Winston noticed a tattoo peeking from the arms of Hugo's rolled-up flannel – the name Anna, inked with what seemed like a real sense of devotion.

"Hugo?" Winston asked, leaning against the doorframe.

"That's me," Hugo replied, his eyes never leaving the windows of his booth.

"I hear you were serving refreshments at the match yesterday," Winston said, trying to keep his tone neutral.

"I was, yeah," Hugo confirmed with a nod, "I often help out there."

"You've been seen leaving work that day, "Winston continued.

"Yeah, I left to go set up the refreshments," Hugo responded.

At first glance, Hugo didn’t seem like the type who would care about a toxicology course, but records indicated he had taken one in the past. Moreover, his work required him to handle complex sound equipment which could involve frequent contact with certain chemicals.

Winston circled back to Hugo's protective side. "You seem close to Anna."

"Yeah," Hugo’s gaze softened, "hee, she's like my baby sister. I've always looked out for her."

Any detective worth his salt knew how protective bonds could drive people to extreme lengths. Winston had heard from others about some cruel remarks Ivy made about ruining Anna and of threats to press charges against her. 

"All right Hugo," Winston said, throwing his coat over his arm, "thank you for your time."

Winston had more pieces to the puzzle now, but he knew the killer wouldn't reveal himself easily. Winston, as always, would be waiting patiently. After all, a game of cat and mouse was half the thrill of his job.

Winston's latest case had piqued his curiosity, leading him to a popular coffee shop downtown where Ivy, the person of interest, was a regular. As he strolled in, the distinct aroma of dark roasted beans permeated the air. Behind the counter, Meredith worked with great efficiency amidst the morning rush. 

"Ivy was a regular here?" Winston questioned and Meredith nodded. "Every morning, like clockwork. Black coffee, a splash of half-and-half. No sugar,” she described Ivy's drink preference.

From a nearby television, a clip replayed on the local news – Ivy, laughing boister⟦ously⟧ whilst imitating some sacred rituals, unmistakenly disrespecting Meredith's beliefs. Winston looked towards Meredith, who now busied herself with a new order – an infusion of a variety of substances readily on hand: chocolate shavings, cinnamon sprinkles, and an endless assortment of flavored syrups.

"Do you mix all the drinks?" Winston asked. Meredith, too preoccupied, responded with a nod. Every shift, Winston noted, Meredith would arrive donning religious symbols around her neck. Today was no exception. As she prepared for her work day, her fingers grazed her amulets and she muttered a silent prayer before diving into the morning pandemonium.

Meredith often spoke publicly about being a staunch follower of her religion and openly declared – more times than Winston would care to count – that anyone who disrespects her beliefs deserves severe punishment.

Right when the morning rush started to wear off, Meredith slipped into the backroom, tugging off her apron. Winston’s eyes landed on a bag near the entrance - a familiar logo from the local butcher shop from where she regularly purchased raw meat.

In the midst of the bustling shop, Winston's attention was drawn to a framed photograph. Meredith was captured mid-spit, a chicken wing in hand.

"But she only buys raw meat," the butcher's words echoed in his mind, contrary to the image he was witnessing. He recalled Meredith’s friends' words: "Meredith has never had cooked meat in front of us."

With lunchtime approaching, the crowd began to ebb and Winston found a moment to delve deeper. In a passing query, he asked, "Heard about the news? Ivy, laughing at your beliefs - that was caught on camera."

Meredith’s hands clenched a coffee cup so tightly it overflowed. In her eyes burned recognition and some suppressed pain. She merely muttered how disrespectful Ivy was.

A customer chimed in, ordering a highly customized drink and Winston’s observation heightened as he watched Meredith expertly mask all traces of the various ingredients she used in the drink. A craft eerily similar to certain practices of subterfuge.

As Winston reached out to accept his coffee—an all-black with a splash of half and half, he pondered over the peculiar pieces of the jig-saw. His goodbye was met with a cautionary note from Meredith, "Hey detective, respect every belief you come across... seems like the world could use more of that, you know?”

As Winston stepped onto the sidewalk, Meredith’s words left him with a chilling twist in his investigation.<turn|>

While examining the photos from the murder scene, Detective Winston couldn't help but feel a chill crawl up his spine. Beneath the bubbles, the crime scene lay at the bottom of the ocean, a place that was supposed to be a sanctuary for divers like Julian.

Coming from a workstation that was perpetually cluttered with stacks of serial killer novels, Clara no doubt had a keen interest in the subject matter. She was frequently engrossed in conversations about infamous serial killers, delving into their modus operandi with unsettling accuracy without any need for references. During her lunch breaks, she could always be found pouring over one of her many true crime books.

Clara, a skilled metal worker, had a specific niche in crafting a variety of unique crowbars, which had become her signature work. Her craftsmanship was distinct and always earned her respect amongst her peers. Going through a surveillance tape, he watched as Clara loaded her uniquely crafted crowbar into her vehicle before heading out to the diving site. The crowbar didn't seem out of place, what with her being a metal worker and competitively acknowledged for her unique metalwork.

Her performance at work had been nothing short of outstanding, and she had been putting in long, overtime hours. She was highly dedicated to her work and never missed an opportunity to express her ambition for a promotion.

Julian and Clara both worked at the same company, and both had been in the running for the same promotion. During the office water cooler chats, he'd heard Clara express her keen interest in the promotion, and her evident disappointment when Julian became a potential contender.

The evidence was laid in front of him: a woman with an enthusiastic interest in killers,⟦ always⟧ reading her crime books even on her lunch breaks, a craftsman with a signature touch on uniquely crafted crowbars, and seen with one on the day of Julian's infamous dive. A metal worker who had been putting in long hours for an impressive performance. All that tied with the delicate balance of coworkers both competing for the same promotion. 

One piece of evidence caught his eye. Clara was also a part of the diving team on the day Julian was murdered. With that, Winston pushed back his chair, stood up, and prepared to pay Clara a visit. He had a feeling there would be more to dig up from her perpetually stacked workspace, files and statements during her interrogation.

Winston stood overlooking the gentle sway of the ocean, the sun reflecting a glaring path of light towards the spot where Julian's body had been found. The dive was a secluded affair, intended just for a small, close-knit group of divers which included Lucy and Julian, often dive partners.

Derailing his thoughts, he flicked through his notes, focusing on Lucy's background - the woman had a varied history, from construction sites to docks, her hand attending to many trades. She'd even taken a boat maintenance course somewhere along the way. A crowbar tool was commonly used in both professions. 

"Detective Winston, Miss Lucy is ready to see you," a uniformed officer approached him. 

"Thank you, officer," he responded, shaking his head in dismissal, his eyes still on the open files in his hand.

He walked into the impromptu interview room, eyes finding Lucy easily. She looked out of place in the cold, steel-colored room, her complexion still holding on to the sun-kissed hue from the sail.

"Lucy," Winston began, his tone neutral. "You and Julian. I've been told you two dive together frequently," he watched her face for any signs of reaction.

"Yes," she confirmed curtly. "Julian and I...we were friends," she added before a tight swallow. "He betrayed my trust though, caused me significant trouble."

That drew his attention. He decided to delve into the more intimate details, "You were managing the tools for this trip?"

Caught off guard, Lucy straightened. "Yes...yes, that's correct. I've always taken care of the gear, packed the crowbar too. Just a precaution..."

"I see. Just a precaution," he repeated.

Catching her eye, he questioned further, "Lucy, did you overhear Julian discussing this betrayal?"

A flicker of shock passed over her face. "Yes...with someone I didn't recognize," she admitted. 

Another clue. He asked, "Lucy, did you find any evidence in Julian's belongings?"

"I... I found some documents in his gear locker...which I always thought only I could access," she confessed.

"Interesting. Very interesting," he nodded before standing up, preparing to leave but not before confirming one last detail.

"You shared the same boat, is that correct?"

In the chilling silence of a hockey rink, Marvin's life was brutally ended with a machete,⟦ leaving⟧ Detective Winston with two elusive suspects: Justin and Frederick.

Detective Winston made his way through the bustling crowds at the local hockey rink. The place had a distinct, chilling atmosphere today, the murder of Marvin casting a grim shadow over it.

He spotted Justin not too far away, watching the game with a fixed expression. Justin had been noticeably depressed since a particular event - he had once proposed to Marvin's fiancé, expressing his undying love, only to be mercilessly rejected. After this incident, he was never quite the same, living with a constant air of despair and refusal to engage with happiness.

"Justin," Winston called out, making his way over. As soon as Justin heard the detective's approach and caught sight of the man in uniform, his eyes instantly lit up, always eager to gain more information about the crime.

"Detective," Justin greeted, his expression somber, yet subtly eager, "here for the game or here about the recent crime?"

Winston raised a brow. Justin seemed too interested. "Any hockey fan would be here for the game," he replied, "Marvin was going to play, wasn't he?"

Justin's dry eyes took on a spark when the murder was mentioned again. He looked dejected at the mention of Marvin, but nodded, "Yeah, he was. I was here to watch it." He had been with the crowd entering the hockey rink at the time of the murder, ready for the game and totally unprepared for the tragedy that eventually unfolded.

He paused, glancing around the rink, then asked, "Do you know how they got in? The murderer, I mean."

Winston kept his expression unreadable, but he noted Justin's quick change of topic back to the crime. "Through the main entrance," he stated simply, "like anyone else," he added, reaffirming that Justin had entered the same way.

"And the time... when exactly did it happen?" Justin changed the topic right back to the crime again, the flame in his eyes burning brighter at the prospect of new details.

Winston frowned slightly, "During the game," he answered, watching Justin's face carefully. He appeared unphased.

Justin cocked a brow, excitement mixed with intrigue evident in his lit eyes. "I was here during that time," he pointed out, "Watching the game."

Winston nodded, "You were, and as far as anyone knows, you didn't leave until well after," he almost sighed, "Listen Justin, what exactly is it with you and this crime? It seems that you're more interested in it than the hockey game."

Justin shifted, looking anywhere but at him, "Well, it's just...Marvin and his fiancé, you know. I just thought they...weren't right for each other. I had a talk with her once. I asked her not to marry him. But she didn't listen."

A sudden clang of a puck hitting the net caught their attention, but Winston kept his gaze on Justin, watching, and listening. There was a lot more to this case than meets the eye, he knew. However, his interview with Justin had just ended, leaving him with more questions than answers.

The harsh, industrial lighting of the hockey rink painted a grave picture as Detective Winston surveyed the crime scene. The rink's security tapes corroborated Frederick's presence at the scene, even capturing a heated argument between him and Marvin. In this particular argument, Marvin was heard threatening harm to Frederick's defenceless daughter. Frederick, a curator of a local weapons museum, also held a job at the hockey rink, giving him a valid reason for being there.

Setting that evidence aside, Winston trotted towards the museum, a place Frederick frequented due to his love for antique machetes. Frederick had the responsibility of overseeing the unique collection of blades, his dedication emanating as bright as the lights above the collection.

What piqued Winston's interest though was that one of the machetes in Frederick's collection matched the description of the weapon that ended Marvin's life. Such violent usage of a machete aligned with Marvin's previous harmful behavior; aggressive threats and unbidden visits to the girls' locker room only added to the growing list of his offensive conduct. After obtaining the necessary legal papers, Winston re-examined the machetes, concluding the lethal weapon indeed came from Frederick's collection.

Taking a break from the museum, Detective Winston investigated Frederick further by questioning those who knew him. His protective behavior for his daughter was a common topic, supported further by a chilling detail given by a coworker in the hockey rink's locker rooms.

"Marvin once threatened Frederick's girl. Frederick didn't take it lightly, and they've been arguing ever since," the coworker confessed. Despite the locker rooms being an area exclusively accessed by staff with keys, Marvin had been spotted in there more times than anyone could count.

Winston's sharp gasp caught the coworkers attention, "What is it, Detective?"

"Nothing...just...let me know if you notice anything else...odd," replied Winston.

Echoes off the old lockers were the only responses he got.

Samuel had been a paramedic, receiving intense training which even included handling emergency situations with injuries from barbed wire. The unfortunate ironic nature of his education was not lost on Winston. He was a man trained to save lives, to handle emergencies. But there had been a serious error during a previous medical procedure, an error Samuel found hard to live down. Now, he made his living in a medical supply store, trying to make up for lost time, perhaps. 

One sunny Monday, Winston himself had seen Samuel, sunglasses shading his eyes, his job posing no hindrance to his apparent penchant for intrigue. Just the next day, the sunglasses had been replaced with eyeglasses. That was a curious detail — Samuel didn't have a prescription for eyewear.

Intriguing, things left to ponder. 

As for the barbed wire, that vile instrument's origin led back to a storage unit. Samuel had a key to said unit. Had he known about its contents? It was, after all, not a common item for city dwellers to come by. 

Then, there was the matter of the hair. Samuel, a typical brown-haired man, had recently been seen sporting hair as dark as the night. A local store clerk had mentioned selling black hair dye to a man fitting Samuel's description days prior. 

Winston remembered mutterings of a superior warning Samuel about potential job loss even jail time. The detective felt a chill run down his spine as he processed the connections. 

A visit to Samuel was in order.
